Magneto-elastic modes and lifetime of magnons in thin yttrium-iron garnet films

Andreas Rückriegel Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik, Universität Frankfurt, Max-von-Laue Strasse 1, 60438 Frankfurt, Germany Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida 32611, USA    Peter Kopietz Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik, Universität Frankfurt, Max-von-Laue Strasse 1, 60438 Frankfurt, Germany Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida 32611, USA    Dmytro A. Bozhko Affiliation: Fachbereich Physik and Landesforschungszentrum OPTIMAS, Technische Universität Kaiserslautern, 67663 Kaiserslautern, Germany    Alexander A. Serga Affiliation: Fachbereich Physik and Landesforschungszentrum OPTIMAS, Technische Universität Kaiserslautern, 67663 Kaiserslautern, Germany    Burkard Hillebrands Affiliation: Fachbereich Physik and Landesforschungszentrum OPTIMAS, Technische Universität Kaiserslautern, 67663 Kaiserslautern, Germany
May 20, 2014
Abstract

We calculate the effects of the spin-lattice coupling on the magnon spectrum of thin ferromagnetic films consisting of the magnetic insulator yttrium-iron garnet. The magnon-phonon hybridisation generates a characteristic minimum in the spin dynamic structure factor which quantitatively agrees with recent Brillouin light scattering experiments. We also show that at room temperature the phonon contribution to the magnon damping exhibits a rather complicated momentum dependence: In the exchange regime the magnon damping is dominated by Cherenkov type scattering processes, while in the long-wavelength dipolar regime these processes are subdominant and the magnon damping is two orders of magnitude smaller. We supplement our calculations by actual measurements of the magnon relaxation in the dipolar regime. Our theory provides a simple explanation of a recent experiment probing the different temperatures of the magnon and phonon gases in yttrium-iron garnet.

I Introduction

Although the spin-lattice interactions in magnetic insulators can often be ignored, in some cases the coupling between the spin degrees of freedom and the lattice vibrations (phonons) plays a crucial role. For example, in ultrasound experiments one uses the spin-lattice coupling to study the properties of the spin degrees of freedom from the measurement of the propagation and the attenuation of sound waves [1]. The theory of magneto-elastic effects in magnetic insulators has been developed more than half a century ago by Abrahams and Kittel [2, 3], and by Kaganov and Tsukernik [4]. While in the past decades a few theoretical studies of magneto-elastic effects have appeared [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10], recent experimental progress in the field of spintronics has revived the interest in the interactions between spin and lattice degrees of freedom [11].

The present work is motivated by an experiment [12] where the coupling between magnons and phonons in the magnetic insulator yttrium iron garnet (YIG) was probed via a spatially resolved measurement of the magnon temperature TmT_{m} in the presence of a thermal gradient. In the short wavelength exchange part of the magnon spectrum TmT_{m} was found to agree almost perfectly with the temperature TpT_{p} of the phonon bath. In order to reconcile this finding with earlier studies of the spin Seebeck effect [13] (which relies on the difference between TmT_{m} and TpT_{p}), the authors of Ref. [12] speculated that in the long-wavelength dipolar part of the spectrum the magnon temperature significantly differs from TpT_{p}, suggesting a rather weak coupling between magnons and phonons in this regime. In this work we offer a microscopic explanation for such a momentum dependence of the magnon temperature: We show that the lifetime τ⁡(𝒌)\tau(\bm{k}) of magnons due to coupling to the phonons in YIG is strongly momentum dependent; in particular τ⁡(𝒌)\tau(\bm{k}) exhibits a pronounced minimum in the exchange regime and is two orders of magnitude larger in the dipolar regime. Since in the dipolar part of the spectrum the magnons have a longer lifetime, in this regime phonons are less effective to thermalize the magnons and the differences between TmT_{m} and TpT_{p} can persist for longer times.

We also present experimental results for the magnon damping in the dipolar regime, which have been obtained by means of time- and wave-vector-resolved Brillouin light scattering (BLS) spectroscopy [14]. The experimentally determined damping rate is three orders of magnitude larger than our theoretical prediction, although the qualitative behavior as a function of in-plane momentum is similar. One should keep in mind, however, that in our calculations only the relaxation due to magnon-phonon interactions has been taken into account. Apparently, in the long-wavelength dipolar regime other scattering channels leading to momentum relaxation are dominant, such as elastic magnon-impurity scattering.

The rest of this work is organized as follows: In Sec. II we briefly review the calculation of the spin wave spectrum of a thin YIG stripe and fix the experimentally relevant parameters. In Sec. III we carefully derive the magnon-phonon interaction by quantizing the phenomenological classical magneto-elastic energy. The calculation of the magneto-elastic modes due to the magnon-phonon hybridisation is presented in Sec. IV. We also calculate the resulting spectral function of the magnons and the transverse dynamic structure factor which is proportional to the BLS cross section. Since we are interested in the magnon dynamics, we derive the effective action of the magnons by integrating over the phonon degrees of freedom. Using this effective action, we proceed in Sec. V to calculate the damping of the magnons due to the coupling to the phonons. We also present new experimental results for the magnon damping in the long-wavelength dipolar regime, and compare them to our calculations. Finally, in Sec. VI we present our conclusions. To make contact with previous work [9] on magnon-phonon interactions in YIG, we present in the appendix an alternative derivation of the dispersion of the magneto-elastic modes using the equations of motion.

III Magnon-phonon Hamiltonian of thin YIG-films

One source of the spin-phonon coupling is the dependence of the true positions 𝒓i=𝑹i+𝑿i\bm{r}_{i}=\bm{R}_{i}+\bm{X}_{i} of the spins on the phonon displacements 𝑿i=𝑿⁡(𝑹i)\bm{X}_{i}=\bm{X}(\bm{R}_{i}) at the lattice sites 𝑹i\bm{R}_{i}. The resulting magnon phonon interaction can be derived from the effective spin-model (1) by expanding the exchange couplings Ji​j=J⁡(𝑹i−𝑹i+𝑿i−𝑿j)J_{ij}=J(\bm{R}_{i}-\bm{R}_{i}+{\bm{X}}_{i}-\bm{X}_{j}) in powers of the phonon displacements [21]. However, in collinear magnets such a procedure does not take into account the dominant source of the magnon-phonon interaction, which is generated by relativistic effects such as dipole-dipole interactions and spin-orbit coupling [9]. These effects involve the charge degrees of freedom so that they cannot be simply included in our effective spin model (1). To derive the proper quantized interaction between magnons and phonons in YIG, we therefore follow the semi-phenomenological approach pioneered by Abrahams and Kittel [2], which relies on the quantization of the phenomenological expression for the classical magneto-elastic energy.

III.2 Quantized magnon-phonon interaction in the Holstein-Primakoff basis

Let us now quantize the magneto-elastic energy. For the phonon field we adopt the usual strategy of expressing the displacement field by the bosonic creation and annihilation operators a𝒌​λ†a^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}\lambda} and a𝒌​λa_{\bm{k}\lambda} of the phonon eigenmodes with momentum 𝒌\bm{k} and polarization 𝒆𝒌​λ\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda},

𝑿⁡(𝒌)\displaystyle\bm{X}(\bm{k}) →\displaystyle\rightarrow VN​𝑿𝒌,\displaystyle\frac{V}{\sqrt{N}}\bm{X}_{\bm{k}}, (24)
𝑿𝒌\displaystyle\bm{X}_{\bm{k}} =\displaystyle= ∑λX𝒌​λ​𝒆𝒌​λ=∑λa𝒌​λ+a−𝒌​λ†2​m​ω𝒌​λ​𝒆𝒌​λ,\displaystyle\sum_{\lambda}X_{\bm{k}\lambda}\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}=\sum_{\lambda}\frac{a_{\bm{k}\lambda}+a^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}\lambda}}{\sqrt{2m\omega_{\bm{k}\lambda}}}\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}, (25)

where λ=1,2,3\lambda=1,2,3 labels the three acoustic phonon branches, ω𝒌​λ=cλ​|𝒌|\omega_{\bm{k}\lambda}=c_{\lambda}|\bm{k}| are the phonon dispersions, mm is the effective ionic mass in a unit cell, VV is the volume of the system, and NN is the number of unit cells. Note that in general the polarization vectors satisfy [24] the orthogonality relations 𝒆𝒌​λ∗⋅𝒆𝒌​λ′=δλ​λ′\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{\ast}\cdot\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda^{\prime}}=\delta_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime}} and the completeness relation ∑λ𝒆𝒌​λ​𝒆𝒌​λ†=𝟏\sum_{\lambda}\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{1}, so that we may identify

Below we shall denote the Fourier transform of the quantized strain tensor by

X𝒌α​β=i2​𝒌α​β⋅𝑿𝒌,𝒌α​β=kα​𝒆β+kβ​𝒆α.X_{\bm{k}}^{\alpha\beta}=\frac{i}{2}\bm{k}_{\alpha\beta}\cdot\bm{X}_{\bm{k}},\;\;\;\bm{k}_{\alpha\beta}=k_{\alpha}\bm{e}_{\beta}+k_{\beta}\bm{e}_{\alpha}. (27)

We may also choose the phases of the unit vectors such that [24] 𝒆𝒌​λ∗=𝒆−𝒌​λ\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{\ast}=\bm{e}_{-\bm{k}\lambda}. For a quasi two-dimensional YIG stripe in the y​zyz-plane we parametrize the in-plane wave vectors as 𝒌=|𝒌|(cos⁡θ𝒌​𝒆z+sin⁡θ𝒌​𝒆y)\bm{k}=|\bm{k}|(\cos\theta_{\bm{k}}\bm{e}_{z}+\sin\theta_{\bm{k}}\bm{e}_{y}), as shown in Fig. 1. A convenient choice for the polarization vectors of the longitudinal and transverse phonons is then

𝒆𝒌∥\displaystyle\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\parallel} =\displaystyle= i(𝒆zcosθ𝒌+𝒆ysinθ𝒌),\displaystyle i(\bm{e}_{z}\cos\theta_{\bm{k}}+\bm{e}_{y}\sin\theta_{\bm{k}}), (28a)
𝒆𝒌⊥1\displaystyle\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\bot 1} =\displaystyle= i(𝒆zsinθ𝒌−𝒆ycosθ𝒌),\displaystyle i(\bm{e}_{z}\sin\theta_{\bm{k}}-\bm{e}_{y}\cos\theta_{\bm{k}}), (28b)
𝒆𝒌⊥2\displaystyle\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\bot 2} =\displaystyle= 𝒆x.\displaystyle\bm{e}_{x}. (28c)

For YIG the relevant value of the effective ionic mass appearing in Eqs. (25, 26) is [9, 20]

m=ρ​a3,ρ=5.17​g/cm3,m=\rho a^{3},\;\;\;\rho=5.17\,{\rm g}/{\rm cm}^{3}, (29)

and the longitudinal and transverse phonon velocities are

c∥=7.209×105​cm/s,c⊥=3.843×105​cm/s.c_{\parallel}=7.209\times 10^{5}\,{\rm cm}/{\rm s},\;\;\;c_{\bot}=3.843\times 10^{5}\,{\rm cm}/{\rm s}. (30)

To quantize the magnetic sector, we follow Refs.[2, 3, 4] and replace the magnetization 𝑴⁡(𝒓)\bm{M}(\bm{r}) at lattice site 𝒓=𝑹i\bm{r}=\bm{R}_{i} by the corresponding spin-operator 𝑺i\bm{S}_{i} according to the prescription

𝑴⁡(𝑹i)→2​μB​n​𝑺i,\bm{M}(\bm{R}_{i})\rightarrow 2\mu_{B}n\bm{S}_{i}, (31)

where n=N/V=1/a3n=N/V=1/a^{3} is the number density. In Fourier space Eq. (31) corresponds to

𝑴(𝒌)→gμBN𝑺𝒌=gμB∑ie−i𝒌⋅𝑹i𝑺i,\bm{M}(\bm{k})\rightarrow g\mu_{B}\sqrt{N}\bm{S}_{\bm{k}}=g\mu_{B}\sum_{i}e^{-i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}_{i}}\bm{S}_{i}, (32)

Assuming that the macroscopic magnetization points along the zz axis, we may express the components of the spin operators at lattice site 𝑹i\bm{R}_{i} in terms of Holstein-Primakoff bosons (magnons) bib_{i} and bi†b_{i}^{\dagger} as usual with Eqs. (3a)–(3c). In momentum space we have

S𝒌z=N​S​δ𝒌,0−1N​∑𝒒b𝒒†​b𝒒+𝒌,S^{z}_{{\bm{k}}}=\sqrt{N}S\delta_{\bm{k},0}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bm{q}}b^{\dagger}_{\bm{q}}b_{\bm{q}+\bm{k}}, (33)

and to leading order in an expansion in powers of 1/S1/S,

S𝒌x\displaystyle S^{x}_{\bm{k}} ≈\displaystyle\approx 2​S2​(b𝒌+b−𝒌†),\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{2S}}{2}(b_{\bm{k}}+b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}}), (34)
S𝒌y\displaystyle S^{y}_{\bm{k}} ≈\displaystyle\approx 2​S2​i​(b𝒌−b−𝒌†).\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{2S}}{2i}(b_{\bm{k}}-b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}}). (35)

For large SS it is reasonable to retain only terms up to quadratic order in the magnons, so that the resulting magneto-elastic Hamiltonian can be written as

ℋme=ℋme(2)+ℋme(3),{\cal{H}}_{\rm me}={\cal{H}}_{{\rm me}}^{(2)}+{\cal{H}}_{{\rm me}}^{(3)}, (36)

where the superscript indicates the number of operators involved. The quadratic term ℋme(2){\cal{H}}_{{\rm me}}^{(2)} is

ℋme(2)\displaystyle{\cal{H}}_{\rm me}^{(2)} =\displaystyle= B⊥​2S​∑𝒌[X−𝒌z​x​(b𝒌+b−𝒌†)−i​X−𝒌z​y​(b𝒌−b−𝒌†)]\displaystyle B_{\bot}\sqrt{\frac{2}{S}}\sum_{\bm{k}}\Bigl[X_{-\bm{k}}^{zx}(b_{\bm{k}}+b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}})-iX_{-\bm{k}}^{zy}(b_{\bm{k}}-b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}})\Bigr] (37)
=\displaystyle= ∑𝒌𝑿−𝒌⋅[𝚪𝒌​b𝒌+𝚪−𝒌∗​b−𝒌†]\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}}\bm{X}_{-\bm{k}}\cdot\left[\bm{\Gamma}_{\bm{k}}b_{\bm{k}}+\bm{\Gamma}^{\ast}_{-\bm{k}}b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}}\right]
=\displaystyle= ∑𝒌[𝑿𝒌∗⋅𝚪𝒌​b𝒌+𝑿𝒌⋅𝚪𝒌∗​b𝒌†],\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}}\left[\bm{X}_{\bm{k}}^{\ast}\cdot\bm{\Gamma}_{\bm{k}}b_{\bm{k}}+\bm{X}_{\bm{k}}\cdot\bm{\Gamma}_{\bm{k}}^{\ast}b^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}\right],

where we have used the fact that the 𝑿𝒌\bm{X}_{\bm{k}} are the Fourier components of a hermitian operator so that

𝑿−𝒌=𝑿𝒌∗,\bm{X}_{-\bm{k}}=\bm{X}_{\bm{k}}^{\ast}, (38)

and the vector vertex 𝚪𝒌\bm{\Gamma}_{\bm{k}} is defined by

𝚪𝒌\displaystyle\bm{\Gamma}_{\bm{k}} =\displaystyle= −B⊥2​S​(𝒌y​z+i​𝒌x​z)\displaystyle-\frac{B_{\bot}}{\sqrt{2S}}\left(\bm{k}_{yz}+i\bm{k}_{xz}\right) (39)
=\displaystyle= −B⊥2​S​[(ky+i​kx)​𝒆z+kz​(𝒆y+i​𝒆x)],\displaystyle-\frac{B_{\bot}}{\sqrt{2S}}\left[(k_{y}+ik_{x})\bm{e}_{z}+k_{z}(\bm{e}_{y}+i\bm{e}_{x})\right],

Expanding

𝑿𝒌=∑λX𝒌​λ​𝒆𝒌​λ,𝚪𝒌=∑λΓ𝒌​λ​𝒆𝒌​λ,\bm{X}_{\bm{k}}=\sum_{\lambda}X_{\bm{k}\lambda}\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda},\;\;\;\bm{\Gamma}_{\bm{k}}=\sum_{\lambda}\Gamma_{\bm{k}\lambda}\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}, (40)

with

X𝒌​λ=𝒆𝒌​λ∗⋅𝑿𝒌,Γ𝒌​λ=𝒆𝒌​λ∗⋅𝚪𝒌,X_{\bm{k}\lambda}=\bm{e}^{\ast}_{\bm{k}\lambda}\cdot\bm{X}_{\bm{k}},\;\;\;\Gamma_{\bm{k}\lambda}=\bm{e}^{\ast}_{\bm{k}\lambda}\cdot\bm{\Gamma}_{\bm{k}}, (41)

the Hamiltonian (37) can be written as

ℋme(2)\displaystyle{\cal{H}}_{\rm me}^{(2)} =\displaystyle= ∑𝒌​λ[Γ𝒌​λ​X𝒌​λ∗​b𝒌+Γ𝒌​λ∗​X𝒌​λ​b𝒌†]\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}\lambda}\left[\Gamma_{\bm{k}\lambda}X^{\ast}_{\bm{k}\lambda}b_{\bm{k}}+\Gamma_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{\ast}X_{\bm{k}\lambda}b^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}\right] (42)
=\displaystyle= ∑𝒌​λX−𝒌​λ​[Γ𝒌​λ​b𝒌+Γ−𝒌​λ∗​b−𝒌†].\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}\lambda}X_{-\bm{k}\lambda}\left[\Gamma_{\bm{k}\lambda}b_{\bm{k}}+\Gamma_{-\bm{k}\lambda}^{\ast}b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}}\right].

This part of the magneto-elastic Hamiltonian describes the hybridisation between the phonon and magnon degrees of freedom. With the choice (28a)–(28c) of the phonon basis we obtain for the projections of the hybridisation vertex

Γ𝒌∥\displaystyle\Gamma_{\bm{k}\parallel} =\displaystyle= i​B⊥2​S​2​ky​kz|𝒌|=i​B⊥2​S​|𝒌|​sin⁡(2​θ𝒌),\displaystyle i\frac{B_{\bot}}{\sqrt{2S}}\frac{2k_{y}k_{z}}{|\bm{k}|}=i\frac{B_{\bot}}{\sqrt{2S}}|\bm{k}|\sin(2\theta_{\bm{k}}), (43a)
Γ𝒌⊥1\displaystyle\Gamma_{\bm{k}\bot 1} =\displaystyle= i​B⊥2​S​ky2−kz2|𝒌|=−i​B⊥2​S​|𝒌|​cos⁡(2​θ𝒌),\displaystyle i\frac{B_{\bot}}{\sqrt{2S}}\frac{k^{2}_{y}-k^{2}_{z}}{|\bm{k}|}=-i\frac{B_{\bot}}{\sqrt{2S}}|\bm{k}|\cos(2\theta_{\bm{k}}),\hskip 19.91692pt (43b)
Γ𝒌⊥2\displaystyle\Gamma_{\bm{k}\bot 2} =\displaystyle= −i​B⊥2​S​kz=−i​B⊥2​S|𝒌|cos⁡θ𝒌.\displaystyle-i\frac{B_{\bot}}{\sqrt{2S}}k_{z}=-i\frac{B_{\bot}}{\sqrt{2S}}|\bm{k}|\cos\theta_{\bm{k}}. (43c)

Before discussing the spectrum of the magneto-elastic modes, let us write down the cubic term ℋme(3){\cal{H}}_{{\rm me}}^{(3)} of the magneto-elastic Hamiltonian in the form [21]

ℋme(3)=1N∑𝒌​𝒌′[𝚪𝒌,𝒌′b¯​b⋅𝑿𝒌−𝒌′b𝒌†b𝒌′\displaystyle{\cal{H}}_{\rm me}^{(3)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}\Bigl[\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{b}b}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\cdot\bm{X}_{\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}}b^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}b_{\bm{k}^{\prime}} (44)
+12!(𝚪𝒌,𝒌′b​b⋅𝑿−𝒌−𝒌′b𝒌b𝒌′+𝚪𝒌,𝒌′b¯​b¯⋅𝑿𝒌+𝒌′b𝒌†b𝒌′†)]\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2!}\left(\bm{\Gamma}^{bb}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\cdot\bm{X}_{-\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}}b_{\bm{k}}b_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}+\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{b}\bar{b}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\cdot\bm{X}_{\bm{k}+\bm{k}^{\prime}}b^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}b^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\right)\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 1N∑𝒌​𝒒𝑿−𝒒⋅[𝑼−𝒒b𝒌†b𝒌+𝒒\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bm{k}\bm{q}}\bm{X}_{-\bm{q}}\cdot\Bigl[\bm{U}_{-\bm{q}}b^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}b_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}
+12!(𝑽−𝒒b−𝒌b𝒌+𝒒+𝑽𝒒∗b𝒌†b−𝒌−𝒒†)],\displaystyle\hskip 39.83385pt+\frac{1}{2!}\left(\bm{V}_{-\bm{q}}b_{-\bm{k}}b_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}+\bm{V}^{\ast}_{\bm{q}}b^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}-\bm{q}}\right)\Bigr],

where the vector vertices are given by

𝚪𝒌,𝒌′b¯​b\displaystyle\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{b}b}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}} =\displaystyle= 𝑼𝒌−𝒌′,\displaystyle\bm{U}_{\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}}, (45a)
𝚪𝒌,𝒌′b​b\displaystyle\bm{\Gamma}^{bb}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}} =\displaystyle= 𝑽𝒌+𝒌′,\displaystyle\bm{V}_{\bm{k}+\bm{k}^{\prime}}, (45b)
𝚪𝒌,𝒌′b¯​b¯\displaystyle\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{b}\bar{b}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}} =\displaystyle= 𝑽−𝒌−𝒌′∗,\displaystyle\bm{V}^{\ast}_{-\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}}, (45c)

with

𝑼𝒒\displaystyle\bm{U}_{\bm{q}} =\displaystyle= i​B∥S​(qx​𝒆x+qy​𝒆y−2​qz​𝒆z),\displaystyle\frac{iB_{\parallel}}{S}(q_{x}\bm{e}_{x}+q_{y}\bm{e}_{y}-2q_{z}\bm{e}_{z}), (46a)
𝑽𝒒\displaystyle\bm{V}_{\bm{q}} =\displaystyle= i​B∥S​(qx​𝒆x−qy​𝒆y)+B⊥S​𝒒x​y\displaystyle\frac{iB_{\parallel}}{S}(q_{x}\bm{e}_{x}-q_{y}\bm{e}_{y})+\frac{B_{\bot}}{S}\bm{q}_{xy} (46b)
=\displaystyle= i​B∥S​(qx​𝒆x−qy​𝒆y)+B⊥S​(qx​𝒆y+qy​𝒆x).\displaystyle\frac{iB_{\parallel}}{S}(q_{x}\bm{e}_{x}-q_{y}\bm{e}_{y})+\frac{B_{\bot}}{S}(q_{x}\bm{e}_{y}+q_{y}\bm{e}_{x}).\hskip 19.91692pt

III.3 Magneto-elastic interaction vertices in the quasi-particle basis

For the calculation of the spectral function of the magnons it is useful to express the magneto-elastic interaction in terms of the magnon quasi-particle operators β𝒌\beta_{\bm{k}} and β𝒌†\beta_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger} which are related to the Holstein-Primakoff bosons b𝒌b_{\bm{k}} and b𝒌†b_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger} via the Bogoliubov transformation (7). Substituting this transformation into Eqs. (37) and (44) we obtain for the hybridisation part

ℋme(2)\displaystyle{\cal{H}}_{\rm me}^{(2)} =\displaystyle= ∑𝒌​λX−𝒌​λ​[Γ𝒌​λβ​β𝒌+Γ−𝒌​λβ¯​β−𝒌†],\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}\lambda}X_{-\bm{k}\lambda}\left[{\Gamma}^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda}\beta_{\bm{k}}+{\Gamma}^{\bar{\beta}}_{-\bm{k}\lambda}\beta^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}}\right], (47)

with

Γ𝒌​λβ\displaystyle{\Gamma}^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda} =\displaystyle= u𝒌​Γ𝒌​λ−v𝒌∗​Γ−𝒌​λ∗,\displaystyle u_{\bm{k}}\Gamma_{\bm{k}\lambda}-v_{\bm{k}}^{\ast}\Gamma^{\ast}_{-\bm{k}\lambda}, (48)
Γ𝒌​λβ¯\displaystyle{\Gamma}^{\bar{\beta}}_{\bm{k}\lambda} =\displaystyle= u𝒌​Γ𝒌​λ∗−v𝒌​Γ−𝒌​λ=(Γ𝒌​λβ)∗.\displaystyle u_{\bm{k}}\Gamma^{\ast}_{\bm{k}\lambda}-v_{\bm{k}}\Gamma_{-\bm{k}\lambda}=({\Gamma}^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda})^{\ast}. (49)

The magnon-phonon interaction defined in Eq. (44) can be written as

ℋme(3)=1N∑𝒌​𝒌′[𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β¯​β⋅𝑿𝒌−𝒌′β𝒌†β𝒌′\displaystyle{\cal{H}}_{\rm me}^{(3)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}\Bigl[\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\cdot\bm{X}_{\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}}\beta^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}\beta_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}
+12!(𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β​β⋅𝑿−𝒌−𝒌′β𝒌β𝒌′+𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β¯​β¯⋅𝑿𝒌+𝒌′β𝒌†β𝒌′†)],\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2!}\left(\bm{\Gamma}^{\beta\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\cdot\bm{X}_{-\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}}\beta_{\bm{k}}\beta_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}+\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{\beta}\bar{\beta}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\cdot\bm{X}_{\bm{k}+\bm{k}^{\prime}}\beta^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}\beta^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\right)\Bigr],

with

𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β¯​β\displaystyle{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\bar{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}} =u𝒌​u𝒌′​𝚪𝒌,𝒌′b¯​b+v𝒌​v𝒌′∗​𝚪−𝒌′,−𝒌b¯​b\displaystyle=u_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\bar{b}b}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}+v_{\bm{k}}v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\bar{b}b}_{-\bm{k}^{\prime},-\bm{k}}
−v𝒌​u𝒌′​𝚪−𝒌,𝒌′b​b−u𝒌​v𝒌′∗​𝚪𝒌,−𝒌′b¯​b¯\displaystyle-v_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{\Gamma}}^{bb}_{-\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}-u_{\bm{k}}v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\bar{b}\bar{b}}_{\bm{k},-\bm{k}^{\prime}}
=(u𝒌​u𝒌′+v𝒌​v𝒌′∗)​𝑼𝒌−𝒌′−v𝒌​u𝒌′​𝑽𝒌′−𝒌−u𝒌​v𝒌′∗​𝑽𝒌′−𝒌∗,\displaystyle\hskip-28.45274pt=(u_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}+v_{\bm{k}}v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}})\bm{U}_{\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}}-v_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\bm{V}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}-\bm{k}}-u_{\bm{k}}v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\bm{V}^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}-\bm{k}}, (51a)
𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β​β\displaystyle{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\beta\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}} =u𝒌​u𝒌′​𝚪𝒌,𝒌′b​b+v𝒌∗​v𝒌′∗​𝚪−𝒌,−𝒌′b¯​b¯\displaystyle=u_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{\Gamma}}^{bb}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}+v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}}v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\bar{b}\bar{b}}_{-\bm{k},-\bm{k}^{\prime}}
−v𝒌∗​u𝒌′​𝚪−𝒌,𝒌′b¯​b−u𝒌​v𝒌′∗​𝚪−𝒌′,𝒌b¯​b\displaystyle-v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\bar{b}b}_{-\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}-u_{\bm{k}}v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\bar{b}b}_{-\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{k}}
=u𝒌​u𝒌′​𝑽𝒌+𝒌′+v𝒌∗​v𝒌′∗​𝑽𝒌+𝒌′∗−(v𝒌∗​u𝒌′+u𝒌​v𝒌′∗)​𝑼−𝒌−𝒌′,\displaystyle\hskip-28.45274pt=u_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{V}}_{\bm{k}+\bm{k}^{\prime}}+v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}}v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{V}}^{\ast}_{\bm{k}+\bm{k}^{\prime}}-(v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}+u_{\bm{k}}v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}})\bm{U}_{-\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}}, (51b)

−u𝒌​v𝒌′​𝚪𝒌,−𝒌′b¯​b−v𝒌​u𝒌′​𝚪𝒌′,−𝒌b¯​b\displaystyle-u_{\bm{k}}v_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\bar{b}b}_{\bm{k},-\bm{k}^{\prime}}-v_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\bar{b}b}_{\bm{k}^{\prime},-\bm{k}}
=u𝒌​u𝒌′​𝑽−𝒌−𝒌′∗+v𝒌​v𝒌′​𝑽−𝒌−𝒌′−(u𝒌​v𝒌′+v𝒌​u𝒌′)​𝑼𝒌+𝒌′.\displaystyle\hskip-28.45274pt=u_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{V}}^{\ast}_{-\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}}+v_{\bm{k}}v_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}{\bm{V}}_{-\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}}-(u_{\bm{k}}v_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}+v_{\bm{k}}u_{\bm{k}^{\prime}})\bm{U}_{\bm{k}+\bm{k}^{\prime}}.
(51c)

Note that the hermiticity of the Hamiltonian implies

𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β¯​β\displaystyle\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}} =\displaystyle= (𝚪𝒌′,𝒌β¯​β)∗,𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β​β=(𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β¯​β¯)∗.\displaystyle(\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{k}})^{\ast}\;,\;\;\;\bm{\Gamma}^{{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}=(\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{\beta}\bar{\beta}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}})^{\ast}. (52)

Below we shall need these interaction vertices to calculate the damping of the magnons in YIG due to the coupling to the phonons. In fact, we shall need the projections of the three-legged vertices onto the phonon basis, which we define by

Γ𝒌,𝒌′,λβ¯​β\displaystyle\Gamma^{\bar{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\lambda} =\displaystyle= 𝒆𝒌′−𝒌,λ∗⋅𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β¯​β\displaystyle\bm{e}^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}-\bm{k},\lambda}\cdot\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}} (53a)
Γ𝒌,𝒌′,λβ​β\displaystyle\Gamma^{{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\lambda} =\displaystyle= 𝒆𝒌′+𝒌,λ∗⋅𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β​β,\displaystyle\bm{e}^{\ast}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{k},\lambda}\cdot\bm{\Gamma}^{{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}, (53b)

or in terms of shifted labels,

Γ𝒌,𝒌+𝒒,λβ¯​β\displaystyle\Gamma^{\bar{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}+\bm{q},\lambda} =\displaystyle= 𝒆𝒒,λ∗⋅𝚪𝒌,𝒌+𝒒β¯​β\displaystyle\bm{e}^{\ast}_{\bm{q},\lambda}\cdot\bm{\Gamma}^{\bar{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}+\bm{q}} (54a)
Γ𝒌,−𝒌+𝒒,λβ​β\displaystyle\Gamma^{{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\lambda} =\displaystyle= 𝒆𝒒,λ∗⋅𝚪𝒌,−𝒌+𝒒β​β.\displaystyle\bm{e}^{\ast}_{\bm{q},\lambda}\cdot\bm{\Gamma}^{{\beta}\beta}_{\bm{k},-\bm{k}+\bm{q}}. (54b)

These vertices should also be useful in microscopic calculations of the non-equilibrium dynamics of magnons in YIG. Note that in Ref. [25] only the Cherenkov type of process described by the vertex 𝚪𝒌,𝒌′β†​β{\bm{\Gamma}}^{\beta^{\dagger}\beta}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}} has been taken into account (however, using a simple phenomenological expression for this vertex). It should be interesting to repeat the calculations of Ref. [25] for the non-equilibrium magnon dynamics in YIG using the more realistic magnon-phonon vertices given above.

IV Magneto-elastic modes in YIG

To calculate the energy dispersion of the magneto-elastic modes, it is sufficient to retain only terms which are quadratic in the magnon and phonon operators. The Hamiltonian of the coupled magnon-phonon system can then be approximated by

ℋ(2)=ℋm(2)+ℋe(2)+ℋme(2),{\cal{H}}^{(2)}={\cal{H}}^{(2)}_{\rm m}+{\cal{H}}^{(2)}_{\rm e}+{\cal{H}}^{(2)}_{\rm me}, (55)

where the quadratic spin wave part ℋm(2){\cal{H}}^{(2)}_{\rm m} is given in Eqs. (5) and (10), the pure phonon part can be written as

ℋe(2)\displaystyle{\cal{H}}^{(2)}_{\rm e} =\displaystyle= ∑𝒌​λ[P−𝒌​λ​P𝒌​λ2​m+m2​ω𝒌​λ2​X−𝒌​λ​X𝒌​λ]\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}\lambda}\left[\frac{P_{-\bm{k}\lambda}P_{\bm{k}\lambda}}{2m}+\frac{m}{2}\omega_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{2}X_{-\bm{k}\lambda}X_{\bm{k}\lambda}\right] (56)
=\displaystyle= ∑𝒌​λω𝒌​λ​[a𝒌​λ†​a𝒌​λ+12],\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}\lambda}\omega_{\bm{k}\lambda}\left[a^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}\lambda}a_{\bm{k}\lambda}+\frac{1}{2}\right],

and the magnon-phonon hybridization ℋme(2){\cal{H}}^{(2)}_{\rm me} is given in Eqs. (42) and (47).

IV.1 Effective magnon action and magnon self-energies

To study the effect of the lattice vibrations on the spin excitations, it is convenient to use a functional integral formulation of the coupled magnon-phonon system and integrate over the phonon degrees of freedom, which in our approximation can be done exactly because we have truncated the expansion (15) of the magneto-elastic energy at the linear order in the phonon coordinates. The magnon operators β𝒌\beta_{\bm{k}} and β𝒌†\beta^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}} in the quasi-particle basis should then be represented by complex fields βK\beta_{K} and β¯K\bar{\beta}_{K} depending on momentum 𝒌\bm{k} and bosonic Matsubara frequency i​ωi\omega, which we collect into the label K=(𝒌,i​ω)K=(\bm{k},i\omega). The resulting Euclidean effective action of the magnons is of the form

S⁡[β¯,β]=S2​[β¯,β]+S3​[β¯,β]+S4​[β¯,β],S[\bar{\beta},\beta]=S_{2}[\bar{\beta},\beta]+S_{3}[\bar{\beta},\beta]+S_{4}[\bar{\beta},\beta], (57)

where the Gaussian part is given by

S2​[β¯,β]\displaystyle S_{2}[\bar{\beta},\beta] =\displaystyle= −1T∑K{[iω−E𝒌−Σ1(K)]β¯KβK\displaystyle-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{K}\Bigl\{\left[i\omega-E_{\bm{k}}-\Sigma_{1}(K)\right]\bar{\beta}_{K}\beta_{K} (58)
−12[Π1(K)β−KβK+Π1∗(K)β¯Kβ¯−K]}.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\left[\Pi_{1}(K)\beta_{-K}\beta_{K}+\Pi_{1}^{\ast}(K)\bar{\beta}_{K}\bar{\beta}_{-K}\right]\Bigr\}.\hskip 19.91692pt

Here the normal and anomalous self-energies to first order in the small parameter 1/S1/S are given by

Σ1​(K)\displaystyle\Sigma_{1}(K) =\displaystyle= −∑λ|Γ𝒌​λβ|2m⁡(ω2+ω𝒌​λ2)=−∑λ|Γ𝒌​λβ|2F0(Kλ),\displaystyle-\sum_{\lambda}\frac{|{\Gamma}^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda}|^{2}}{m(\omega^{2}+\omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda})}=-\sum_{\lambda}|{\Gamma}^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda}|^{2}F_{0}({K\lambda}),
Π1​(K)\displaystyle\Pi_{1}(K) =\displaystyle= −∑λΓ𝒌​λβ​Γ−𝒌​λβm⁡(ω2+ω𝒌​λ2)=−∑λΓ𝒌​λβΓ−𝒌​λβF0(Kλ),\displaystyle-\sum_{\lambda}\frac{{\Gamma}^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda}{\Gamma}^{\beta}_{-\bm{k}\lambda}}{m(\omega^{2}+\omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda})}=-\sum_{\lambda}{\Gamma}^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda}{\Gamma}^{\beta}_{-\bm{k}\lambda}F_{0}({K\lambda}),

where we have introduced the symmetric phonon propagator

F0​(K​λ)=1m⁡(ω2+ω𝒌​λ2).F_{0}({K\lambda})=\frac{1}{m(\omega^{2}+\omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda})}. (61)

The interference of the magnon-phonon hybridisation with the cubic term of the magneto-elastic coupling yields a cubic contribution to the effective magnon-magnon interaction,

S3​[β¯,β]\displaystyle S_{3}[\bar{\beta},\beta] =\displaystyle= −1T​N∑K1​K2​K3δK1+K2+K3,0[\displaystyle-\frac{1}{T\sqrt{N}}\sum_{K_{1}K_{2}K_{3}}\delta_{K_{1}+K_{2}+K_{3},0}\Bigr[ (62)

+13!Γ123β​β​ββ1β2β3+13!Γ123β¯​β¯​β¯β¯−1β¯−2β¯−3],\displaystyle\hskip-31.29802pt+\frac{1}{3!}\Gamma^{\beta\beta\beta}_{123}\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\beta_{3}+\frac{1}{3!}\Gamma^{\bar{\beta}\bar{\beta}\bar{\beta}}_{123}\bar{\beta}_{-1}\bar{\beta}_{-2}\bar{\beta}_{-3}\Bigr],

Here δK,K′=δ𝒌,𝒌′​δω,ω′\delta_{K,K^{\prime}}=\delta_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\delta_{\omega,\omega^{\prime}} and for simplicity we have abbreviated β1≡βK1\beta_{1}\equiv\beta_{K_{1}} and ΓK1;K2​K3β¯​β​β≡Γ1;23β¯​β​β\Gamma^{\bar{\beta}\beta\beta}_{K_{1};K_{2}K_{3}}\equiv\Gamma^{\bar{\beta}\beta\beta}_{1;23}, and similarly for the other labels. IV.2 Magnon spectral function and dynamic structure factor

Due to the off-diagonal self-energy Π⁡(K)\Pi(K) generated by the magnon-phonon interaction, the magnon Green function has also an off-diagonal component, so that we should consider the normal and anomalous propagators. In terms of the normal irreducible self-energies the normal magnon propagator can be written as

G⁡(K)\displaystyle G(K) =\displaystyle= −T⁡⟨βK​β¯K⟩=−i​ω+E𝒌+Σ⁡(−K)D⁡(K),\displaystyle-T\langle\beta_{K}\bar{\beta}_{K}\rangle=-\frac{i\omega+E_{\bm{k}}+\Sigma(-K)}{D(K)},\hskip 19.91692pt (68)

while the anomalous magnon propagator is

P⁡(K)\displaystyle P(K) =\displaystyle= −T⁡⟨βK​β−K⟩=Π∗​(K)D⁡(K).\displaystyle-T\langle\beta_{K}{\beta}_{-K}\rangle=\frac{\Pi^{\ast}(K)}{D(K)}. (69)

Here

D⁡(K)=−[i​ω−Σ−​(K)]2+[E𝒌+Σ+​(K)]2−|Π⁡(K)|2,D(K)=-[i\omega-\Sigma_{-}(K)]^{2}+[E_{\bm{k}}+\Sigma_{+}(K)]^{2}-|\Pi(K)|^{2}, (70)

can be identified with the determinant of the inverse matrix Green function, and

Σ±​(K)=12​[Σ⁡(K)±Σ⁡(−K)].\Sigma_{\pm}(K)=\frac{1}{2}\left[\Sigma(K)\pm\Sigma(-K)\right]. (71)

The spectrum of the magneto-elastic modes can be obtained from the roots of the equation

D⁡(𝒌,ω+i​η)=0,D(\bm{k},\omega+i\eta)=0, (72)

with infinitesimal positive η\eta. Hence, the magneto-elastic modes are determined by

[ω−Σ−​(𝒌,ω)]2−E𝒌2−2​E𝒌​Σ+​(𝒌,ω)\displaystyle[\omega-\Sigma_{-}(\bm{k},\omega)]^{2}-E_{\bm{k}}^{2}-2E_{\bm{k}}\Sigma_{+}(\bm{k},\omega) (73)
=\displaystyle= [Σ+​(𝒌,ω)]2−|Π⁡(𝒌,ω)|2.\displaystyle[\Sigma_{+}(\bm{k},\omega)]^{2}-|\Pi(\bm{k},\omega)|^{2}.

For large effective spin SS we may approximate the self-energies by the first order corrections given in Eqs. (IV.1) and (IV.1). Using the explicit polarization basis given in Eqs. (28a)–(28c) it is easy to see that Σ−​(K)=0\Sigma_{-}(K)=0 in this approximation, so that we may identify Σ+​(K)=Σ​(K)\Sigma_{+}(K)=\Sigma(K). Still, Eq. (73) amounts in general to finding the solutions of a sixth order polynomial. However, the last two terms on the right hand side involving the square of the self-energies are of order 1/S21/S^{2} and can be neglected; we have checked numerically that these terms do not have any significant effect for the parameters relevant to YIG. The equation for the magneto-elastic modes then reduces to

ω2−E𝒌2=2​E𝒌​Σ1​(𝒌,ω),\omega^{2}-E_{\bm{k}}^{2}=2E_{\bm{k}}\Sigma_{1}(\bm{k},\omega), (74)

where Σ1​(𝒌,ω)\Sigma_{1}(\bm{k},\omega) is defined in Eq. (IV.1). To further simplify this equation let us assume that either the energy of the longitudinal phonon mode or the energy of the transverse phonon modes is close to the magnon energy E𝒌E_{\bm{k}}. In the first case we may approximate

Σ1​(𝒌,ω)≈|Γβ𝒌∥|2m(ω2−ω𝒌∥2),\Sigma_{1}(\bm{k},\omega)\approx\frac{|\Gamma^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\parallel}|^{2}}{m(\omega^{2}-\omega_{\bm{k}\parallel}^{2})}, (75)

while in the second case

Σ1​(𝒌,ω)≈|Γ𝒌⊥β|2m⁡(ω2−ω𝒌⊥2),\Sigma_{1}(\bm{k},\omega)\approx\frac{|\Gamma^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\bot}|^{2}}{m(\omega^{2}-\omega_{\bm{k}\bot}^{2})}, (76)

where

|Γ𝒌⊥β|2=|Γ𝒌⊥,1β|2+|Γ𝒌⊥,2β|2.|\Gamma^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\bot}|^{2}=|\Gamma^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\bot,1}|^{2}+|\Gamma^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\bot,2}|^{2}. (77)

Eq. (74) is then bi-quadratic and has the solutions

Ω𝒌​λ±2=ω𝒌​λ2+E𝒌22±(ω𝒌​λ2−E𝒌2)24+Δ𝒌​λ4,\Omega_{\bm{k}\lambda\pm}^{2}=\frac{\omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda}+E^{2}_{\bm{k}}}{2}\pm\sqrt{\frac{(\omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda}-E^{2}_{\bm{k}})^{2}}{4}+\Delta_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{4}}, (78)

where

Δ𝒌​λ4\displaystyle\Delta_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{4} =\displaystyle= 2​E𝒌m​|Γ𝒌​λβ|2.\displaystyle 2\frac{E_{\bm{k}}}{m}|\Gamma^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda}|^{2}. (79)

The energy dispersion of these modes is shown graphically in Fig. 2 for 𝒌=k​𝒆z\bm{k}=k\bm{e}_{z} parallel to the in-plane magnetic field.

Note that for this propagation direction the longitudinal phonon does not hybridise with the magnon dispersion because for ky=0k_{y}=0 (corresponding to θ𝒌=0\theta_{\bm{k}}=0) the relevant hybridisation function Γ𝒌∥\Gamma_{\bm{k}\parallel} given in Eq. (43a) vanishes.

The normal component of the magnon Green function is in this approximation

G⁡(𝒌,i​ω)\displaystyle G(\bm{k},i\omega) =\displaystyle= i​ω+E𝒌+Σ1​(𝒌,i​ω)(i​ω)2−E𝒌2−2​E𝒌​Σ1​(𝒌,i​ω).\displaystyle\frac{i\omega+E_{\bm{k}}+\Sigma_{1}(\bm{k},i\omega)}{(i\omega)^{2}-E_{\bm{k}}^{2}-2E_{\bm{k}}\Sigma_{1}(\bm{k},i\omega)}. (80)

If i​ωi\omega is close to ω𝒌​λ\omega_{\bm{k}\lambda} this can be approximated by

G⁡(𝒌,i​ω)\displaystyle G(\bm{k},i\omega) ≈\displaystyle\approx [i​ω+E𝒌]​[(i​ω)2−ω𝒌​λ2]+|Γ𝒌​λβ|2m[(i​ω)2−E𝒌2]​[(i​ω)2−ω𝒌​λ2]−2​E𝒌​|Γ𝒌​λβ|2m.\displaystyle\frac{[i\omega+E_{\bm{k}}][(i\omega)^{2}-\omega_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{2}]+\frac{|\Gamma^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda}|^{2}}{m}}{[(i\omega)^{2}-E_{\bm{k}}^{2}][(i\omega)^{2}-\omega_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{2}]-2E_{\bm{k}}\frac{|\Gamma^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda}|^{2}}{m}}.\hskip 28.45274pt (81)

After analytic continuation to the real frequency axis we obtain for the corresponding spectral function

A⁡(𝒌,ω)=−1π​Im​G​(𝒌,ω+i​η)\displaystyle A(\bm{k},\omega)=-\frac{1}{\pi}{\rm Im}G(\bm{k},\omega+i\eta) (82)
≈\displaystyle\approx Z𝒌​λ(ω)∑s=±s[δ(ω−Ω𝒌​λ​s)+δ(ω+Ω𝒌​λ​s)],\displaystyle Z_{\bm{k}\lambda}(\omega)\sum_{s=\pm}s[\delta(\omega-\Omega_{\bm{k}\lambda s})+\delta(\omega+\Omega_{\bm{k}\lambda s})],\hskip 19.91692pt

where

Z𝒌​λ​(ω)=[ω+E𝒌]​[ω2−ω𝒌​λ2]+|Γ𝒌​λβ|2m2​ω​[Ω𝒌​λ+2−Ω𝒌​λ−2].Z_{\bm{k}\lambda}(\omega)=\frac{[\omega+E_{\bm{k}}][\omega^{2}-\omega_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{2}]+\frac{|\Gamma^{\beta}_{\bm{k}\lambda}|^{2}}{m}}{2\omega[\Omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda+}-\Omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda-}]}. (83)

An intensity plot of the magnon spectral function for YIG is shown in Fig. 3. One clearly sees the transfer of spectral weight between the magnon and the phonon branch at the crossing point.

Actually, the Brillouin light scattering intensity is proportional to the transverse spin structure factor [27, 26]

S⊥​(𝒌,ω)=∫−∞∞d​t2​π​ei​ω​t​⟨S−𝒌x​(0)​S𝒌x​(t)+S−𝒌y​(0)​S𝒌y​(t)⟩,S_{\bot}(\bm{k},\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{2\pi}e^{i\omega t}\langle S^{x}_{-\bm{k}}(0)S^{x}_{\bm{k}}(t)+S^{y}_{-\bm{k}}(0)S^{y}_{\bm{k}}(t)\rangle, (84)

where the Fourier transform of the spin-operator is defined in Eq. (32). To leading order in spin wave theory we obtain

S⊥​(𝒌,ω)\displaystyle S_{\bot}(\bm{k},\omega) =\displaystyle= S1−e−ω/T\displaystyle\frac{S}{1-e^{-\omega/T}}
×{(u𝒌2+|v𝒌|2)[A(−𝒌,ω)−A(𝒌,−ω)]\displaystyle\times\Bigl\{(u_{\bm{k}}^{2}+|v_{\bm{k}}|^{2})\left[A(-\bm{k},\omega)-A(\bm{k},-\omega)\right]
−2(u𝒌v𝒌∗+u𝒌v𝒌)B(𝒌,ω)},\displaystyle-2\left(u_{\bm{k}}v^{\ast}_{\bm{k}}+u_{\bm{k}}v_{\bm{k}}\right)B(\bm{k},\omega)\Bigr\},

is the spectral function of the anomalous magnon Green function P⁡(𝒌,i​ω)P(\bm{k},i\omega), which for imaginary frequencies is defined by Eq. (69). We obtain

B⁡(𝒌,ω)\displaystyle B(\bm{k},\omega) ≈\displaystyle\approx Y𝒌​λ(ω)∑s=±s[δ(ω−Ω𝒌​λ​s)+δ(ω+Ω𝒌​λ​s)],\displaystyle Y_{\bm{k}\lambda}(\omega)\sum_{s=\pm}s[\delta(\omega-\Omega_{\bm{k}\lambda s})+\delta(\omega+\Omega_{\bm{k}\lambda s})],

where

Y𝒌​λ​(ω)=−Γ−𝒌⊥,1β¯​Γ𝒌⊥,1β¯+Γ−𝒌⊥,2β¯​Γ𝒌⊥,2β¯2​m​ω​[Ω𝒌​λ+2−Ω𝒌​λ−2].Y_{\bm{k}\lambda}(\omega)=-\frac{\Gamma^{\bar{\beta}}_{-\bm{k}\bot,1}\Gamma^{\bar{\beta}}_{\bm{k}\bot,1}+\Gamma^{\bar{\beta}}_{-\bm{k}\bot,2}\Gamma^{\bar{\beta}}_{\bm{k}\bot,2}}{2m\omega[\Omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda+}-\Omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda-}]}. (88)

An intensity plot of the transverse dynamic structure factor is shown in Fig. 4.

Note that the qualitative behavior is very similar to the behavior of the magnon spectral function, which is due to the fact that the Bogoliubov transformation has only a small effect because of the smallness of the Boguliubov coefficient v𝒌v_{\bm{k}} in the entire Brillouin zone.

V Magnon damping

In this section we calculate the decay rate (i.e., the damping) of the magnons due to the magnon-phonon interaction in YIG at room temperature. The damping γ⁡(𝒌)\gamma({\bm{k}}) of magnons with wave vector 𝒌\bm{k} and energy E𝒌E_{\bm{k}} can be obtained from the imaginary part of the self-energy Σ⁡(K)=Σ⁡(𝒌,i​ω)\Sigma(K)=\Sigma(\bm{k},i\omega) after analytic continuation to the real frequency axis,

γ(𝒌)=−ImΣ(𝒌,iω→E𝒌+iη).\gamma(\bm{k})=-{\rm Im}\Sigma(\bm{k},i\omega\rightarrow E_{\bm{k}}+i\eta). (89)

To leading order in 1/S1/S the damping is determined by the second order self-energy given in Eq. (66); after carrying out the frequency sum we obtain

V.1 Dipolar regime: Theory

In the long-wavelength regime |𝒌|≲Δ/ρs|\bm{k}|\lesssim\sqrt{\Delta/\rho_{s}} the behavior of the magnon damping (92) strongly depends on the size v⁡(𝒌)=|𝒗⁡(𝒌)|v(\bm{k})=|\bm{v}(\bm{k})| of the group velocity 𝒗⁡(𝒌)=∇𝒌E𝒌\bm{v}(\bm{k})=\nabla_{\bm{k}}E_{\bm{k}} of the magnons in comparison with the phonon velocities. In Fig. 6 we show the momentum range where the magnon velocity v⁡(𝒌)v(\bm{k}) exceeds the phonon velocities cλc_{\lambda}.

In regime around the minima of the dispersion, the velocity v⁡(𝒌)v(\bm{k}) is small compared with the phonon velocities, while at very small wave vectors v⁡(𝒌)>cλv(\bm{k})>c_{\lambda}. In this regime around the minima of the dispersion the decay rate the magnons is dominated by the confluent process given in Eq. () because the Cherenkov processes are kinematically suppressed. In fact, in a substantial regime around dispersion minima the quasi-particle velocity is small compared with the phonon velocities, so that we may approximate E−𝒌+𝒒≈E𝒌−𝒗⁡(𝒌)⋅𝒒E_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q}}\approx E_{\bm{k}}-\bm{v}(\bm{k})\cdot\bm{q} and expand the decay rate in powers of v⁡(𝒌)/cλv(\bm{k})/c_{\lambda}. The momentum integration in Eq. () can then be carried out and we obtain

The confluent contribution to the high-temperature damping rate in the dipolar regime is shown graphically as the thin dotted line in Fig. 7. On the other hand, the Cherenkov-type process contributes only for very small 𝒌\bm{k}, when v⁡(𝒌)≳cλv(\bm{k})\gtrsim c_{\lambda}, see Fig. 6. However, for those momenta it is no longer valid to linearize the dispersion due to the strong effect of the Bogoliubov transformation, and no analytical approximation can be obtained. Therefore we only present the numerical solution as dashed line in Fig. 7. Obviously, apart from an enhancement for k≲2×104​cm−1k\lesssim 2\times 10^{4}\,{\rm cm}^{-1} the damping exhibits a rather weak dependence on the wave vector in this regime.

V.2 Dipolar regime: Experiment

For a comparison of our calculation with experiments one should keep in mind that we have only considered the contribution from the magnon-phonon interactions on the damping of the magnons. Of course, in the real system there are other sources leading to magnon decay, such as magnon-magnon interactions or the elastic scattering of magnons by impurities. We therefore expect that the magnon damping due to magnon-phonon interactions is a lower limit to the experimentally observed magnon damping rate. In fact, our experimental data presented below show that in the dipolar regime magnon-phonon interactions are not the dominant source of magnon damping.

In order to determine the relaxation time of different groups of magnons, a measurements of the spectral distribution of magnon gas densities as a function of the frequency and wave vector using time- and wave-vector-resolved BLS spectroscopy [14] has been performed. Due to technical reasons only in-plane wave vectors from 00 up to the kzmax=11×104​cm−1k_{z}^{\rm max}=11\times 10^{4}\,{\rm cm}^{-1} are accessible within our apparatus. The measurements were performed using a YIG film with thickness 6.7​μ6.7\,\mum, which was liquid-phase epitaxialy grown on a 500​μ500\,\mum thick gallium gadolinium garnet substrate.

The magnon spectrum was populated by intensive thermalization [28, 25, 29] of magnons, which were injected by the parallel parametric pumping technique [30] at half of the pumping frequency fp=13.62f_{p}=13.62\,GHz. The bias magnetic field of H=1710H=1710\,Oe was tuned to provide the excitation of parametric magnons at the ferromagnetic resonance frequency. In this case the direct transition of magnons to the bottom of spin wave spectrum is prohibited by conservation laws. This ensures high efficiency of multi-stage four-magnon scattering which is necessary for thermalization and thus population of the spectrum.

We have measured the redistribution of thermalized magnons along the fundamental backward-volume magnetostatic spin wave mode as a function of time and wave vector. After switching off the pumping, the magnons are allowed to relax freely. By fitting the relaxation times for different groups of thermalized magnons we were able to extract the damping rates. The obtained dependence of measured total damping rate γtot\gamma_{\rm tot} on the in-plane wave vector for dipolar-exchange spin waves is shown in Fig. 8. Obviously, the value of relaxation rate is roughly three orders of magnitude larger than our calculated relaxation rate due to magnon-phonon interactions shown Fig. 7. We thus conclude that in the long-wavelength dipolar regime other relaxation channels (in particular two-magnon scattering processes[31, 32, 34, 33]) dominate the magnon damping. The rather irregular behavior of the measured damping rate in Fig. 8 suggests that elastic scattering of magnons by impurities might play an important role in this regime. Note that within the tolerance limits of the experiment the measured relaxation rate has a rather weak dependence on the in-plane wave vectors in the entire accessible range of wave vectors. In this respect the experimental results agree with our prediction of a momentum-independent damping rate in this regime.

Unfortunately, microscopic calculations of the magnon decay rates at room temperature, taking magnon-impurity and magnon-magnon interactions into account, are not available in the momentum range relevant for our experiment. One should keep in mind, however, that magnon-impurity scattering can only explain the momentum-relaxation of the magnon gas; for the equilibration of the different temperatures of the magnon and the phonon systems magnon-phonon interactions are essential.

The confluent contribution to the high-temperature damping rate in the exchange regime is shown graphically as the thin dotted line in Fig. 9. As one can see, the magnon damping is strongly 𝒌\bm{k} dependent. In particular, it exhibits peaks at the crossing points of magnon and phonon dispersions as well as velocities. It also increases by two orders of magnitude between dipolar and exchange regimes, which are dominated by confluence and Cherenkov processes respectively. For the magnon lifetime τ⁡(𝒌)=1/(2​π​γ​(𝒌))\tau(\bm{k})=1/(2\pi\gamma(\bm{k})), this implies values of the order of 50​μ​s50\,{\rm\mu s} in the dipolar momentum range, while it can be as low as 480​ns480\,{\rm ns} for exchange momenta.

VI Summary and conclusions

In this work we have studied magneto-elastic interactions in experimentally relevant thin films of the magnetic insulator YIG. As the dominant sources of magneto-elastic interactions are due to relativistic effects [9] which cannot be taken into account within an effective model containing only spin degrees of freedom, we have used a semi-phenomenological approach [2], which relies on the quantization of a suitable phenomenological expression for the magneto-elastic energy. For the quantized theory we have then carefully derived the momentum dependence of the magneto-elastic interaction vertices within the framework of the conventional 1/S1/S-expansion for ordered quantum spin systems. Using these vertices, we have explicitly calculated the leading contributions to the hybridisation between magnon and phonon modes, as well as the damping of the magnons due to spin-lattice coupling. The hybridisation has been shown to give rise to a characteristic minimum in the spin dynamic structure factor at the crossing point of magnon and transversal phonon dispersions, where the spectral weight is transferred from the magnons to the transverse phonon mode. The position of this minimum quantitatively agrees with the recent experimental observation of the magneto-elastic mode [35].

The damping at room temperature has been shown to be strongly momentum dependent. In the long-wavelength dipolar regime it is rather flat and almost exclusively driven by confluent magnon-phonon scattering processes where two magnons decay into a phonon or vice versa. In this regime, we have also presented new experimental results for the magnon damping obtained by wave-vector-resolved Brillouin light scattering spectroscopy. The fact that the experimental results for the magnon damping are roughly three orders of magnitude larger than our theoretical results indicate that in the dipolar regime magnon-phonon interactions are not the dominant source of magnon damping in our samples at room temperature. We suspect that in this regime the magnon damping is dominated by elastic scattering of magnons from impurities. On the other hand, in the short-wavelength exchange regime the damping is due to magnon-phonon scattering processes of the Cherenkov type and is two orders of magnitude larger than in the dipolar regime. The damping rate exhibits pronounced peaks at the crossing points of magnon and phonon dispersions and velocities. This agrees very well with the conclusions of the experiment [12], where the authors suggested that the spin-lattice relaxation in the dipolar regime should be much slower than in the exchange regime in order to reconcile their results with earlier work on the spin Seebeck effect.

The present work can be extended in two directions: on the theoretical side, it would be useful to have quanitatively accurate calculations of the magnon damping due to magnon-impurity and magnon-magnon interactions in the dipolar regime; we expect that this can provide a better explanation for our experimental results shown in Fig. 8, which is three orders of magnitude larger than the damping due to magnon-phonon interactions in this regime. Note, however, that recently Chernyshev [36] has considered spontaneous magnon decays of the 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0 magnon in YIG due to magnon-magnon interactions in high magnetic fields. On the experimental side, it would be useful to measure magnon damping in the exchange regime and compare the data with our theoretical prediction shown in Fig. 9.

APPENDIX: MAGNETO-ELASTIC MODES FROM EQUATIONS OF MOTION

In this appendix we show how to obtain the energy dispersions of the magneto-elastic modes from the linearized equations of motion of the coupled magnon-phonon system. Although our derivation using the effective magnon action presented in Sec. IV is simpler, the derivation in this appendix is more in the spirit of previous work [9] using classical equations of motion.

To obtain the energy dispersions of the eigenmodes we write down the Heisenberg equations of motion of both the Holstein-Primakoff bosons and the phonon operators. Within the linear approximation we have

i​b˙𝒌\displaystyle i\dot{b}_{\bm{k}} =\displaystyle= A𝒌​b𝒌+B𝒌​b−𝒌†+𝚪𝒌∗⋅𝑿𝒌,\displaystyle A_{\bm{k}}b_{\bm{k}}+B_{\bm{k}}b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}}+\bm{\Gamma}^{\ast}_{\bm{k}}\cdot\bm{X}_{\bm{k}}, (A1a)
−i​b˙−𝒌†\displaystyle-i\dot{b}^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}} =\displaystyle= A𝒌​b−𝒌†+B𝒌​b𝒌+𝚪−𝒌⋅𝑿𝒌,\displaystyle A_{\bm{k}}b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}}+B_{\bm{k}}b_{\bm{k}}+\bm{\Gamma}_{-\bm{k}}\cdot\bm{X}_{\bm{k}}, (A1b)
X˙𝒌​λ\displaystyle\dot{X}_{\bm{k}\lambda} =\displaystyle= P𝒌​λm,\displaystyle\frac{P_{\bm{k}\lambda}}{m}, (A2a)
P˙𝒌​λ\displaystyle\dot{P}_{\bm{k}\lambda} =\displaystyle= −m​ω𝒌​λ2​X𝒌​λ−Γ𝒌​λ​b𝒌−Γ−𝒌​λ∗​b−𝒌†.\displaystyle-m\omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda}X_{\bm{k}\lambda}-\Gamma_{\bm{k}\lambda}b_{\bm{k}}-\Gamma^{\ast}_{-\bm{k}\lambda}b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}}. (A2b)

It is useful to express the equations of motion for the Holstein-Primakoff bosons in terms of the transverse spin components, which to leading order in the 1/S1/S-expansion can be identified with

S𝒌x\displaystyle S^{x}_{\bm{k}} =\displaystyle= 2​S2​(b𝒌+b−𝒌†),\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{2S}}{2}\left(b_{\bm{k}}+b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}}\right), (A3)
S𝒌y\displaystyle S^{y}_{\bm{k}} =\displaystyle= 2​S2​i​(b𝒌−b−𝒌†).\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{2S}}{2i}\left(b_{\bm{k}}-b^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}}\right). (A4)

Then Eqs. (A1a) and (A1b) can be written as

S˙𝒌x\displaystyle\dot{S}^{x}_{\bm{k}} =\displaystyle= (A𝒌−B𝒌)​S𝒌y+i​B⊥​𝒌y​z⋅𝑿𝒌,\displaystyle(A_{\bm{k}}-B_{\bm{k}})S^{y}_{\bm{k}}+iB_{\bot}\bm{k}_{yz}\cdot\bm{X}_{\bm{k}}, (A5a)
S˙𝒌y\displaystyle\dot{S}^{y}_{\bm{k}} =\displaystyle= −(A𝒌+B𝒌)​S𝒌x−i​B⊥​𝒌x​z⋅𝑿𝒌,\displaystyle-(A_{\bm{k}}+B_{\bm{k}})S^{x}_{\bm{k}}-iB_{\bot}\bm{k}_{xz}\cdot\bm{X}_{\bm{k}}, (A5b)

while the phonon momenta satisfy

P˙𝒌​λ\displaystyle\dot{P}_{\bm{k}\lambda} =\displaystyle= −m​ω𝒌​λ2​X𝒌​λ+i​B⊥S​𝒆𝒌​λ∗⋅(𝒌x​z​S𝒌x+𝒌y​z​S𝒌y),\displaystyle-m\omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda}X_{\bm{k}\lambda}+i\frac{B_{\bot}}{S}{\bm{e}}^{\ast}_{\bm{k}\lambda}\cdot\left(\bm{k}_{xz}S^{x}_{\bm{k}}+\bm{k}_{yz}S^{y}_{\bm{k}}\right),

implying

X¨𝒌​λ+ω𝒌​λ2​X𝒌​λ=i​B⊥m​S​𝒆𝒌​λ∗⋅(𝒌x​z​S𝒌x+𝒌y​z​S𝒌y).\displaystyle\ddot{X}_{\bm{k}\lambda}+\omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda}X_{\bm{k}\lambda}=i\frac{B_{\bot}}{mS}{\bm{e}}^{\ast}_{\bm{k}\lambda}\cdot\left(\bm{k}_{xz}S^{x}_{\bm{k}}+\bm{k}_{yz}S^{y}_{\bm{k}}\right). (A7)

If we ignore the magnon-phonon coupling, we obtain from Eqs. (A5a,A5b),

S¨α𝒌+E𝒌2Sα𝒌=0,α=x,y,\ddot{S}^{\alpha}_{\bm{k}}+E_{\bm{k}}^{2}{S}^{\alpha}_{\bm{k}}=0,\;\;\;\alpha=x,y, (A8)

where the magnon dispersion in the absence of phonons is given in Eq. (9). With finite magnon-phonon hybridization we obtain the energies of the magneto-elastic modes from the roots of the secular determinant of the above equations of motion. For simplicity, let us assume that the energy of only one particular phonon mode ω𝒌​λ\omega_{\bm{k}\lambda} is close to E𝒌E_{\bm{k}}. To calculate the energy of the magneto-elastic mode close to the crossing point, it is then sufficient to approximate 𝑿𝒌≈X𝒌​λ​𝒆𝒌​λ\bm{X}_{\bm{k}}\approx X_{\bm{k}\lambda}\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda} in the above equations of motion. Then we obtain the energies of the magneto elastic modes from the roots of the following quartic secular equation,

(ω2−ω𝒌​λ2)​(ω2−E𝒌2)\displaystyle(\omega^{2}-\omega_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{2})(\omega^{2}-E_{\bm{k}}^{2}) (A9)
=\displaystyle= B⊥2m​S{(A𝒌+B𝒌)|𝒌y​z⋅𝒆𝒌​λ|2+(A𝒌−B𝒌)|𝒌x​z⋅𝒆𝒌​λ|2\displaystyle\frac{B_{\bot}^{2}}{mS}\Bigl\{(A_{\bm{k}}+B_{\bm{k}})|\bm{k}_{yz}\cdot\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}|^{2}+(A_{\bm{k}}-B_{\bm{k}})|\bm{k}_{xz}\cdot\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}|^{2}
+2ωIm[(𝒌x​z⋅𝒆𝒌​λ)(𝒌y​z⋅𝒆𝒌​λ∗)]}.\displaystyle\hskip 19.91692pt+2\omega{\rm Im}\left[(\bm{k}_{xz}\cdot\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda})(\bm{k}_{yz}\cdot\bm{e}^{\ast}_{\bm{k}\lambda})\right]\Bigr\}.

For the phonons in a thin YIG stripe the basis vectors 𝒆𝒌​λ\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda} can always be chosen such that the last term in Eq. (A9) vanishes, so that the secular equation is bi-quadratic and can be explicitly solved. The square of the energies of the magneto-elastic modes in a thin YIG stripe are therefore

(Ω𝒌​λ±)2=ω𝒌​λ2+E𝒌22±(ω𝒌​λ2−E𝒌2)24+Δ𝒌​λ4,(\Omega^{\pm}_{\bm{k}\lambda})^{2}=\frac{\omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda}+E^{2}_{\bm{k}}}{2}\pm\sqrt{\frac{(\omega^{2}_{\bm{k}\lambda}-E^{2}_{\bm{k}})^{2}}{4}+\Delta_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{4}}, (A10)

where

Δ𝒌​λ4\displaystyle\Delta_{\bm{k}\lambda}^{4} =\displaystyle= B⊥2[(A𝒌+B𝒌)|𝒌y​z⋅𝒆𝒌​λ|2m​S\displaystyle B_{\bot}^{2}\Bigl[(A_{\bm{k}}+B_{\bm{k}})\frac{|\bm{k}_{yz}\cdot\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}|^{2}}{mS} (A11)
+(A𝒌−B𝒌)|𝒌x​z⋅𝒆𝒌​λ|2m​S].\displaystyle\hskip 11.38109pt+(A_{\bm{k}}-B_{\bm{k}})\frac{|\bm{k}_{xz}\cdot\bm{e}_{\bm{k}\lambda}|^{2}}{mS}\Bigr].

If we approximate B𝒌≈0B_{\bm{k}}\approx 0 (which corresponds to neglecting quantum fluctuations generated by the dipolar interaction) Eq. (A10) agrees with the result obtained via the classical equations of motion [9].
